data.title: Targeting the biology of ageing with mTOR inhibitors to improve immune function in older adults: phase 2b and phase 3 randomised trials
data.authors: Mannick JB; Teo G; Bernardo P; Quinn D; Russell K; Klickstein L; Marshall W; Shergill S

evidence.label: Human study
evidence.note: this describes the kind of study, not its quality

data.finding: This paper reports two trials of RTB101, a drug that blocks mTOR, taken once a day for 16 weeks by adults over 65. In the phase 2b trial (652 people), fewer people on 10 mg had a lab-confirmed respiratory infection than on placebo (19% against 28%), but that result comes from a pooled analysis the authors did not correct for multiple testing, and the corrected analysis did not reach significance. The phase 3 trial (1,024 people) used a different main endpoint, set with the FDA: symptoms with or without a lab test. It found no difference (26% against 25%, p = 0.65), although blood tests still showed more antiviral genes switched on in both trials. In phase 2b, twice-daily dosing and a combination with everolimus did not reach significance, which the authors read as a hint that on-off inhibition may beat constant inhibition. Those numbers are "data not shown" in the paper. Boundary: RTB101 is not rapamycin or everolimus, the phase 3 group was healthier (no COPD, no smokers), and that trial was too small to test the lab-confirmed endpoint. The only everolimus arm (RTB101 plus everolimus 0.1 mg daily) was a combination and did not reach significance, which is why this paper is listed against the everolimus and immune function link on the pathway map. It cannot show what everolimus alone does.
data.abstract_excerpt: The COVID-19 pandemic highlights the need for therapies that improve immune function in older adults, including interferon (IFN)-induced antiviral immunity that declines with age. In a previous phase 2a trial, RTB101 (previously known as BEZ235), an oral mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) inhibitor, was observed to increase IFN-induced antiviral gene expression and decrease the incidence of respiratory tract infections (RTIs) in older adults.

extracted_findings.effect: Phase 3 FAILED its primary endpoint (no reduction in symptomatic respiratory infections, 26 vs 25%); antiviral genes still upregulated
extracted_findings.dose: RTB101 5 or 10 mg once daily (+/- everolimus in phase 2b); phase 3 used RTB101 10 mg once daily; oral, placebo-controlled.
extracted_findings.sample_size: Phase 2b + phase 3 across >1500 adults aged >=65 (phase 3 n=1024).
extracted_findings.effect_size: Phase 3 primary endpoint (proportion with >=1 clinically symptomatic respiratory illness) NOT met; RTB101 still upregulated IFN-induced antiviral gene expression. Biomarker moved, clinical outcome did not.
extracted_findings.limitations: FDA changed the primary endpoint between phase 2b and phase 3 (symptom-based vs lab-confirmed), complicating comparison; positive biomarker did not translate to clinical benefit.

extracted_findings_review.note: AI-assisted extraction from the paper. The curated finding takes precedence where the two disagree.
